Sampras, now 37 and an American famed for his lightning-fast serves that earned him the moniker 'Pistol Pete,' claimed 14 grand slam singles crowns throughout his 15-year career—a record at the time—yet the Roland Garros title always eluded him.

By defeating Sweden's Robin Soderling 6-1, 7-6, 6-4 on Sunday to claim the French crown, Federer drew level with Sampras and joined an exclusive club as just the sixth man ever to triumph at all four major tournaments.

In Sampras's view, this achievement establishes the 27-year-old Swiss as the sport's ultimate competitor: "The things he's accomplished in the last five years have simply never happened before—and I doubt they'll ever be repeated."

"Whether or not he'd won there, he still ranks as the best there's ever been. This victory merely proves it," Sampras remarked to the Guardian newspaper.

"Naturally I'm delighted for Roger. If anyone deserves this, he does. He'd been agonizingly close before," Sampras said of the freshly minted champion and current world number two, who had fallen to Spain's Rafael Nadal in the previous three French Open finals in a row.

Speaking to CNN alone following his triumph, Federer admitted his relief at recovering from a difficult period in 2008, when Nadal had taken over his top ranking as well as his Australian Open and Wimbledon crowns.

"It's been a wonderful day—finally securing this French title that had escaped me for so long feels incredible. I always trusted that I had the ability to win it, but actually lifting the trophy, considering everything I'd endured, is just remarkable. The pride I'm feeling right now is beyond words."

"Retiring was never something I contemplated. I put in enormous effort during the off-season. Suddenly, reaching semifinals and finals wasn't enough to satisfy people anymore. But this win comes at the perfect moment because I've shown all those doubters they were mistaken."

The significance of making history wasn't overlooked by Federer either: "These records are hugely important to me, particularly after these past few years when it dawned on me that I belonged among the sport's all-time greats. Breaking records is something I genuinely enjoy—since I've always admired figures like Sampras, Agassi, Connors, and McEnroe, standing alongside them is truly special."

Yet in a foreboding message to his competitors, the champion made clear he was already focused on future goals: "I sense there's plenty more in the tank—I'm just 27 and I'd love to keep competing for many more seasons, and hopefully collect plenty more titles along the way."

Soderling, who Federer had beaten in the final, also had glowing words for the man who defeated him: "In my opinion he's the greatest ever, and I'd know, having faced him so many times," the world number 12 told CNN.

Federer's next challenge is the 2009 season's third major, Wimbledon, beginning June 22, where he'll seek to surpass Bjorn Borg's mark by claiming the title for a sixth time.

Federer's momentous weekend triumph also drew recognition from International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Jacques Rogge, who likewise labeled the Swiss the finest tennis has ever produced. "I sent Roger Federer a note today congratulating him on this extraordinary accomplishment, because in my eyes he stands as the greatest player of all time," Rogge stated during a press conference in Brussels on Monday.

The IOC chief disclosed that his letter also voiced hope that Federer would compete at London's 2012 Olympic Games. Federer had already claimed an Olympic gold medal to his impressive résumé last year in Beijing, winning the men's doubles alongside his fellow Swiss Stanislas Wawrinka.

**PARIS —** Roger Federer finally conquered the one mountain that had eluded him, capturing his first French Open title Sunday with a 6-1, 7-6(1), 6-4 victory over Robin Söderling, completing a career Grand Slam and etching his name alongside the greatest players in tennis history.

"Last year was probably the most difficult of my career," Federer reflected in the press conference following his win. "I was struggling with mononucleosis early in the season, and people were writing me off. "After Wimbledon last year, that final against Rafa, it took something out of me," Federer admitted. "To lose in the dark, in five sets, after holding all those break points—it was heartbreaking. But I told myself the story wasn't finished."

Federer's path to the final was aided by an extraordinary turn of events when Söderling stunned four-time champion Nadal in the fourth round, removing the Spaniard who had defeated Federer in the previous three Paris finals.

"This is a dream come true," he said finally. "The French Open was the missing piece. Now I know that whatever happens in my career, I've completed something very few players ever will. But I'm not done yet. Not by a long way."

# Federer Equals Sampras's Grand Slam Record with French Open Triumph

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — Roger Federer captured his first French Open title on Sunday, defeating his opponent in straight sets at Roland Garros to claim his 14th Grand Slam singles title and equal Pete Sampras's all-time record.

The Swiss star's victory in Paris completes his career Grand Slam, making him one of only a handful of men in tennis history to win all four major championships. The clay-court title had long eluded Federer, who had suffered previous final defeats at the tournament.

"This is the greatest moment of my career," Federer said after the match. "To win here in Paris, on the surface I've struggled with most, and to reach Pete's record—it's a dream come true."

## Completing the Collection

The French Open had become something of a nemesis for Federer, the one prize missing from his glittering trophy cabinet. With this triumph, he joins the elite group of players to have conquered all four Grand Slam surfaces.

Sampras, whose record of 14 major titles had stood as the benchmark for greatness in men's tennis, offered his congratulations to Federer on matching his achievement.

## Olympic Gold and Beyond

The Roland Garros victory caps a remarkable period for the Swiss maestro, who claimed Olympic gold in the men's doubles at the Beijing Games alongside compatriot Stanislas Wawrinka. While singles success had eluded him at the Olympics, the doubles triumph added another prestigious title to his résumé.

## Eyes on Wimbledon

Attention now turns to Wimbledon, where Federer will look to surpass Sampras's record outright at the All England Club—the venue where he has enjoyed some of his greatest triumphs.

Federer has been a dominant force on the grass courts of southwest London, and a victory at the upcoming Championships would see him claim a record-breaking 15th Grand Slam title.

"Wimbledon is special to me," Federer added. "To have the chance to make history there would mean everything."

The tennis world will be watching closely as Federer seeks to etch his name permanently into the record books.
